chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ali from Amr ibn Sa'id from Musaddiq ibn Sadah from Ammar ibn Musa from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

Regarding a man who prays over two or three dead bodies, how should he pray over them? He said: 'If there are three, or two, or ten, or more than that, he should pray one prayer over them, saying five takbirs over them just as he prays over one dead person, having prayed over them all. He places one dead body, then places the next against the buttocks of the first, then places the head of the third against the buttocks of the second, like a staircase, until he finishes with all of them, whatever their number. When he has arranged them thus, he stands in the middle and says five takbirs, doing as he does when he prays over one dead person.'

He was asked: 'If they are dead men and women?' He said: 'He begins with the men, placing the head of the second against the buttocks of the first until he finishes with all the men. Then he places the head of the woman against the buttocks of the last man, then places the head of the other woman against the head of the first woman, until he finishes with all of them. When he has arranged them thus, he stands in the middle, in the middle of the men, says takbir and prays over them just as he prays over one dead person.'

He was asked about a dead person over whom prayer was offered, and when the Imam said salam, the dead person was found upside down, his feet towards the place of his head. He said: 'He is straightened and the prayer is repeated over him, if he has been carried but not yet buried. If he has been buried, then the prayer has passed and no prayer is offered over him while he is buried.'
ai.seo_question: How does one perform the funeral prayer for multiple deceased people according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* establishes the principle of congregational unity in funeral prayers, allowing a single Imam to pray over multiple deceased by arranging them in a continuous line or stack. It provides precise jurisprudential details for mixed-gender arrangements and distinguishes between valid and invalid prayers based on whether the body was buried or merely carried after being found upside down. This reflects the Shia emphasis on the completeness of the ritual act even when performed collectively.
